A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GAUSS/JAC tall-data inference work. Inspection of all 49 pages of v2 and 52 pages of v3 supports matching the methods, equations, experiments and appendices, including relocated material and the new Appendix M.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulation experiments on Gaussian toy models, SBI benchmarks and the Jansen–Rit neural mass model, with runtime, posterior-accuracy, robustness and diagnostic results.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds comparisons with a deterministic sampler, including explicitly rerun experiments in Appendix M.

M1.justification: GAUSS and JAC retain their covariance approximations, precision-weighted score combination and DDIM sampling procedure. Their algorithm numbers are exchanged. The score-network architecture, training objective, classifier-free guidance and partial-factorization extensions are retained; expanded explanations do not establish a new proposed procedure.

E1.justification: The Gaussian/GMM toys, three principal SBI benchmarks, additional Appendix I tasks and both JRNMM variants already appear in v2. Appendix M evaluates another sampler on retained tasks. The more explicit JRNMM description and relocated 4D results do not add dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix M adds Geffner et al.'s deterministic sampler, DET_GEF, to runtime and accuracy comparisons on the toy models and SLCP, Lotka–Volterra and SIR, including clipped variants in benchmark plots. This substantially extends comparison beyond the retained Langevin baseline and existing tamed-ULA analysis.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported injected score perturbation from epsilon times (1-alpha_t) to epsilon times sqrt(1-alpha_t). This is a reported setting revision, without establishing that the retained main-text plots were rerun. Appendix M specifies 1000 steps for DET_GEF alongside the retained 1000-step GAUSS and 400-step JAC/Langevin comparison.

E4.justification: Appendix M extends controlled score-noise and stability comparisons to DET_GEF. New Figure 10 supplies reference-versus-GAUSS posterior pairplots for SLCP, Lotka–Volterra and SIR. Existing dimensionality, clipping, tamed-ULA, classifier-free guidance and partial-factorization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The retained runtime-ratio Table 2 changes its uncertainty description from confidence intervals in v2 to mean and standard deviation over five seeds in v3. v3 also explains that toy-model seeds correspond to different sampled parameters. Existing benchmark and local-C2ST replication procedures remain; increased run counts are not reported.

E6.justification: Appendix M adds substantial runtime and accuracy results while retaining the original main comparisons. Table 8 reports DET_GEF as fastest, with a runtime ratio of 0.22 relative to Langevin at dimension 10. Figure 25 shows its advantage over GAUSS for low-noise GMM at larger observation counts, alongside GAUSS's greater noise robustness. These are additional comparisons and reruns, with possible seed/GPU variation explicitly acknowledged.

T1.justification: The two central lemmas and their main derivations remain. Local mathematical revisions include making Lemma 3.2 explicitly approximate, changing a residual F-term sign in Appendix A.2, and changing the DDIM denoising-mean factor from sqrt(alpha_t) to its reciprocal. Appendix M.1 adds mathematical comparison of the reverse kernels and Gaussian/isotropic equivalence conditions.

C1.justification: Both versions claim Langevin-free tall-posterior sampling from single-observation score estimates through second-order backward-kernel approximations, with improved speed and stability demonstrated on toy models, SBI benchmarks and JRNMM. The rewritten abstract, introduction and conclusion preserve this central contribution and application scope.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands interpretation beyond v2's existing tuning and error-accumulation discussion. Table 3 and Appendix H explain task-dependent metric strengths and limitations. Appendix M distinguishes low-noise accuracy from practical stability and attributes instability to systematic score bias amplified by posterior contraction, including for deterministic sampling. The conclusion adds specific stabilization and large-context scalability directions.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies JRNMM dynamics, numerical prior bounds and 33-bin log-PSD summaries, plus the clipping threshold and Langevin step-size formula. These document existing experiments. Conversely, Appendix E drops the explicit beta(t)=32t schedule and detailed MALA initialization/adaptation instructions. Most network, training and code-access information remains.

R1.justification: Section 3.2 and Appendix M substantially extend positioning against the deterministic alternative in the already-cited Geffner et al. paper, emphasizing covariance preservation and Gaussian-limit behavior. v3 also connects future work to Gloeckler, Rissanen and Arruda et al. (2025), alongside additional background citations.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, method explanations and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v3 introduces dedicated NPSE and algorithms subsections, moves the DDIM derivation into Appendix C, incorporates positive-definiteness discussion into Appendix A, and restructures Appendix J. Acknowledgements and the impact statement are removed.

P2.justification: v3 adds metric/result summary tables, posterior pairplots and DET_GEF comparison plots, and expands Figure 1 with an n=64 panel. It moves the runtime-ratio table and 4D JRNMM result into the main text, combines existing diagnostic panels, and extensively resizes and repaginates figures under a changed document layout.

improvement.justification: The previously omitted deterministic comparator makes the speed, accuracy and stability tradeoffs easier to assess, while clearer explanations and JRNMM settings improve usability. These gains are tempered by deleted MALA/noise-schedule details and new internal inconsistencies: the DDIM summary in Equations 5–6 differs from Appendix C, and Equation 49 uses variance where Section 2.1 uses its square root for noise scaling. The resulting overall improvement is limited.
